scripts.clear: gjsify clear lib tsconfig.tsbuildinfo tsconfig.types.tsbuildinfo test.gjs.mjs test.node.mjs
scripts.build: gjsify run build:gjsify && gjsify run build:types
scripts.build:test: gjsify run build:test:gjs && gjsify run build:test:node
scripts.test: gjsify run build:gjsify && gjsify run build:test && gjsify run test:node && gjsify run test:gjs

osNotes.darwin: `os.cpus()` reports the documented all-zero `times` on macOS. Linux reads the per-CPU tick counters from `/proc/stat`; the darwin equivalent is Mach's `host_processor_info(PROCESSOR_CPU_LOAD_INFO)`, which GJS cannot call without a native bridge, and no userland tool prints the cumulative per-core totals Node returns (`top`/`iostat` give an instantaneous aggregate percentage). Every other export — cpus model/speed, memory, uptime, loadavg, networkInterfaces, userInfo — is real on darwin and covered by the macOS suites. `src/index.spec.ts` carries the matching `it.failing(…, { when })`, so the claim retires itself the day a reader exists.
osNotes.win32: A `src/win32.ts` covers the per-platform answers, but it is unexercised for the same structural reason as `@gjsify/child_process`: `runtimes.node: "none"` sends `test:node` to native Node, and there is no GJS host on Windows to run `test:gjs`. Measured on the win11-gjsify VM: 10 of 178 specs fail there, and all ten are POSIX assumptions in the SPECS (asserting `type()` is `Linux`, EOL is `\n`, devNull is `/dev/null`) rather than defects in this module.
